title: KDP PDF Upload Takes Forever? Here's How to Fix Slow Processing
description: A practical troubleshooting guide for Amazon KDP PDF uploads that hang, process forever, or fail because of oversized files, Canva exports, high-resolution images, transparency, and browser limits.
metaTitle: KDP PDF Upload Takes Forever? Fix Stuck Processing
metaDescription: Amazon KDP upload stuck processing forever? Fix slow PDF uploads, oversized coloring books, Canva exports, and manuscript processing errors fast.
ogTitle: KDP PDF Upload Takes Forever? Fix Slow Processing
ogDescription: Learn why Amazon KDP uploads hang or process forever, and how to repair oversized PDFs, Canva exports, image-heavy manuscripts, and slow cover uploads.
ogImageAlt: KDP PDF upload troubleshooting workflow for slow processing and stuck manuscript uploads.
excerpt: If your manuscript or cover PDF uploads to Amazon KDP and then sits on a spinner forever, the file is usually fixable. This guide explains why KDP processing slows down and how to optimize oversized PDFs, Canva exports, coloring books, and image-heavy interiors without rebuilding the whole book.
author: KDP Preflight Editorial
shortAnswer: When a KDP PDF upload takes forever, the cause is usually not Amazon rejecting your book. It is usually an oversized or complex PDF: full-page PNGs, 600 DPI artwork, unflattened transparency, bloated Canva exports, mismatched trim or bleed, or a browser running out of memory. Optimize images to about 300 DPI at final print size, flatten complex pages, re-export a clean print PDF, then test small page ranges to find the problem page.

faqs.question: Why is my KDP upload taking so long?
faqs.answer: A KDP upload usually takes too long because the PDF is very large, image-heavy, unflattened, exported poorly, or difficult for KDP to rasterize. Coloring books, puzzle books, photo books, and Canva exports are common causes.

faqs.question: What PDF size is too large for KDP?
faqs.answer: KDP can accept large PDFs, but risk rises sharply once a manuscript is over about 150 MB to 200 MB, especially if every page is a full-page image. A 300 MB to 500 MB coloring book often needs image optimization before upload.

faqs.question: Can Canva exports slow down KDP?
faqs.answer: Yes. Canva can create unnecessarily large PDFs when a design contains giant backgrounds, duplicated images, transparent layers, shadows, and full-page PNG artwork. Exporting as PDF Print is correct, but the source assets still need to be sized intelligently.

faqs.question: Why does my upload freeze at processing?
faqs.answer: Processing freezes when KDP receives the file but struggles to analyze or render it. The usual causes are oversized images, corrupted pages, unflattened transparency, embedded font problems, trim or bleed mismatches, or temporary KDP server delays.

faqs.question: Does KDP have a file size limit?
faqs.answer: Amazon KDP has upload limits that can change by format and workflow, so check the current KDP Help pages before relying on a number. In practice, you should optimize well before the limit because huge valid files can still process slowly.

faqs.question: Should I flatten my PDF before upload?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the book uses transparency, shadows, glow effects, layered vectors, or complex Canva elements. Flattening simplifies the file KDP has to render while preserving the visible page when done at print quality.

faqs.question: Why do coloring books upload slowly?
faqs.answer: Coloring books often upload slowly because each page is a full-page raster image. If those images are oversized PNGs, 600 DPI exports, AI-upscaled artwork, or transparent pages, the final manuscript can become extremely heavy.

faqs.question: Can huge PNG files break KDP?
faqs.answer: Huge PNG files can make KDP processing very slow or unstable. PNG is useful for transparency and sharp line art, but full-page PNGs on every page can create a massive PDF. Flatten finished pages and use only the resolution needed for print.

faqs.question: Is 600 DPI too high for KDP?
faqs.answer: For most KDP print books, 600 DPI is unnecessary and can make uploads much slower. Use about 300 DPI at final printed size unless you have a specific line-art workflow that requires more detail.

faqs.question: How long should KDP processing normally take?
faqs.answer: A clean text-heavy PDF may process in a few minutes. Image-heavy manuscripts and covers can take longer. If processing has not moved after 20 to 30 minutes, optimize the PDF, test a smaller page range, and try a clean browser session.

summary: Slow KDP uploads usually come from file complexity, not from a mysterious publishing account problem.
The highest-impact fixes are image resizing, PDF flattening, clean export settings, and split-testing small page ranges to find the problematic asset.
KDPPreflight helps catch oversized pages, dimension mismatches, bleed mistakes, and risky exports before you spend another upload cycle waiting on Amazon.
checklist: The manuscript PDF is not unnecessarily large for the book type.
Full-page images are close to 300 DPI at final print size, not 600 DPI or larger without reason.
Coloring book pages are flattened and not stored as giant transparent PNGs.
Canva exports use PDF Print and are not converted repeatedly after download.
Fonts are embedded and the PDF opens cleanly in a local PDF viewer.
Trim size, bleed choice, and cover setup match the KDP project settings.
The file was tested in a clean browser or private window with fewer tabs open.
Problem pages were isolated by uploading 10-page and 50-page test PDFs.
The final file was validated before uploading again.

howTo.name: How to fix a KDP PDF upload that takes forever
howTo.description: A step-by-step workflow for repairing slow Amazon KDP manuscript and cover uploads caused by oversized PDFs, Canva exports, image-heavy pages, transparency, and browser limits.

steps.name: Check the PDF size and page type
steps.text: Confirm whether the file is text-heavy, image-heavy, or built from full-page raster images. Large coloring books, puzzle books, and photo books need closer inspection.

steps.name: Resize source images
steps.text: Reduce oversized images to about 300 DPI at their final printed size. Avoid placing 6000 pixel artwork on pages that only need 2550 pixels for print.

steps.name: Flatten complex pages
steps.text: Flatten transparency, shadows, glow effects, and layered artwork before upload so KDP does not have to resolve complex rendering during processing.

steps.name: Re-export a clean print PDF
steps.text: Use Canva PDF Print or a professional print PDF preset with embedded fonts and correct trim or bleed dimensions.

steps.name: Split-test the manuscript
steps.text: Upload a 10-page test PDF, then a 50-page test PDF, then the full file. This isolates corrupted or unusually heavy pages.

content: If your KDP PDF upload takes forever, the waiting is maddening because Amazon gives you very little useful feedback. The bar moves, the spinner keeps spinning, the manuscript says processing, or the cover upload appears to finish and then hangs.

This happens often with image-heavy books. Coloring books are especially vulnerable because every page may be a full-page image. Puzzle books, photo books, planners with textured backgrounds, children books, and Canva-made interiors can hit the same wall.

Most slow uploads are caused by a small group of fixable issues: huge PDFs, oversized images, bad exports, browser memory issues, and problematic transparency layers. The file may look fine on your computer, but KDP still has to upload, inspect, rasterize, and render it inside Amazon publishing workflow.
Your file is usually fixable without redesigning the whole book. The goal is not to crush the PDF until it looks bad. The goal is to remove processing weight that does not improve the printed book.
## Why KDP Uploads Become Extremely Slow

Amazon KDP does more than store the PDF after you click upload. For print books, KDP has to scan the file, read page boxes, process fonts, inspect images, validate trim size, check bleed, compare the cover and interior settings, calculate spine width, rasterize pages for preview, and generate a browser-based proof.

A text-only paperback is easy for that pipeline. A 120-page coloring book where every page is a full PNG is very different. A photo book with large images on every page is heavier again. A Canva export with large backgrounds, shadows, transparent stickers, duplicated assets, and rasterized text can be technically valid but slow to process.

The slow part is often not the upload itself. Your browser may send the PDF to Amazon, then the file sits in KDP manuscript processing slow mode while Amazon tries to render it. That is why some people say the upload reached 100 percent but KDP processing forever never ends.

KDP also has to reconcile the book setup. If your selected trim size is 8.5 x 11 but the manuscript PDF is another size, KDP has more validation work to do. If the cover was built for an old page count, spine calculation can add another failure point. For layout-specific issues, see the guide to [interior and cover file mismatch on KDP](/blog/interior-and-cover-file-dont-match-kdp) and the [trim mismatch troubleshooting guide](/blog/kdp-cover-size-does-not-match-interior).

The first visual on this page, kdp-upload-processing-pipeline.webp in the content plan, is represented in the app as a lightweight responsive SVG diagram with the alt meaning: How Amazon KDP processes uploaded PDF interiors and covers. The second optimization visual shows why a huge image-heavy PDF can be reduced without harming print quality.
## The Most Common Causes of Slow KDP Uploads
### Oversized PDF Files

Oversized PDFs are the most common cause of Amazon KDP upload stuck problems. The file may be 200 MB, 320 MB, or even 500 MB, and it may still open locally. Local viewing is not the same as KDP processing. Your computer can display cached pages one at a time; KDP has to analyze the whole print file and prepare it for Previewer.

Coloring books often become huge when every page is exported as one full-page PNG. A 100-page 8.5 x 11 interior can balloon quickly if each page contains a 5000 or 7000 pixel image. That extra data usually does not make the printed page better. At 300 DPI, an 8.5 inch wide page needs roughly 2550 pixels across before bleed. A 6000 pixel wide raster page adds a lot of processing weight.

A realistic range for many simple text-heavy books is under 25 MB. Journals and puzzle books may sit around 20 MB to 80 MB depending on artwork. Coloring books often work well between 40 MB and 150 MB when the pages are optimized. Photo books may legitimately be larger, but once a manuscript is over 200 MB, slow processing becomes much more likely.

File size alone is not the only signal. A 120 MB flattened print PDF may upload better than an 80 MB PDF with broken transparency and malformed fonts. Still, if your KDP PDF too large problem starts with a 320 MB manuscript, optimization is the right first move.
### Canva Export Problems

Canva is popular for KDP because it is approachable, but Canva often creates unnecessarily large PDFs. A design may look simple while the exported PDF contains large hidden backgrounds, duplicated image assets, transparent layers, shadows, glow effects, and rasterized page groups.

PDF Print is usually the right Canva export option for KDP. The mistake is assuming PDF Print can rescue every source file. If you placed a giant PNG on every page, added transparent overlays, duplicated the same full-page texture hundreds of times, and then exported the book, PDF Print preserves a lot of that weight.

Canva also encourages visual layering. A coloring page might include a white page background, a transparent PNG illustration, a subtle paper texture, decorative corner art, page numbers, and shadows. Multiply that by 100 pages and KDP has a lot to flatten during processing.

A practical Canva workflow is to keep the design print-sized from the beginning, avoid unnecessary full-page backgrounds, use vector elements where possible, delete hidden or off-canvas assets, export as PDF Print, and avoid running the exported PDF through several online converters afterward.
### Too Many High-Resolution Images

Print quality matters, but more resolution is not always better. KDP print files normally need images around 300 DPI at final printed size. A 600 DPI image can be useful for certain line-art workflows, but it often hurts upload performance when used across an entire manuscript.

Think in printed inches. A 6 x 9 full-page image at 300 DPI needs about 1800 x 2700 pixels. An 8.5 x 11 full-page image needs about 2550 x 3300 pixels. If your interior page is 8.5 inches wide and the placed image is 7000 pixels wide, KDP receives far more data than the printed page can use.

This is especially common with AI-upscaled artwork. A creator generates coloring pages, upscales them dramatically, downloads each page as a transparent PNG, places every page into Canva, then exports one huge PDF. The book may be visually simple black line art, but technically it is a massive stack of oversized raster images.

The resolution comparison visual, kdp-resolution-comparison.webp in the content plan, maps to the in-app DPI diagram below. Its alt meaning is: Comparison between optimal and excessive image resolution for KDP PDFs.

If your problem is blurry output rather than a slow upload, read [how to fix low resolution images on KDP](/blog/fix-low-resolution-images-kdp) and [why your KDP cover looks blurry after upload](/blog/why-your-kdp-cover-looks-blurry-after-upload). Resolution and file weight are related, but they are not the same problem.
### Transparency and Layer Problems

Transparency is one of the quietest causes of KDP upload hangs. Semi-transparent elements, shadows, glow effects, layered vectors, multiply effects, soft masks, and unflattened assets all require rendering decisions. Your design app may handle those decisions instantly because it knows the original layers. KDP receives the final PDF and has to interpret them.

Complex transparency is common in Canva covers, illustrated children books, low-content interiors with textured pages, and journals with decorative backgrounds. It can also appear in professional files from Photoshop, Illustrator, Affinity, or InDesign if the export leaves effects live.

Flattening finished artwork simplifies the file. It does not mean flattening text into blurry screenshots. It means resolving visual effects at print quality so KDP does not have to calculate them during processing. Done correctly, flattening can make the PDF smaller, more predictable, and easier for KDP to render.
### Browser or Device Limitations

Sometimes the PDF is acceptable and the local browser is the weak link. KDP upload and Previewer run inside a web browser. Large files can trigger memory spikes, especially on low-RAM laptops or browsers that have been open for days.

Multiple open tabs, browser extensions, ad blockers, password managers, PDF plugins, and old cached KDP sessions can interfere. This is why incognito mode is not generic throwaway advice. A private window reduces extensions and stale browser state, giving you a cleaner test.

Before rebuilding the book, try a clean browser test. Restart the browser. Open KDP in incognito or private mode. Close heavy tabs. Disable extensions for the session. If possible, try another browser or another computer. If the same file works elsewhere, the blocker was likely browser-side. If it fails everywhere, focus on the PDF.
## Step-by-Step Fixes That Actually Work
### Compress Images Before Export

The best KDP slow upload fix usually happens before the final PDF is created. Do not take a huge PDF, smash it through the most aggressive online compressor, and hope for the best. That can damage line art, soften photos, rasterize text, and create new PDF problems.

Instead, inspect the source images. Full-page 6 x 9 images should usually be near 1800 x 2700 pixels. Full-page 8.5 x 11 images should usually be near 2550 x 3300 pixels. Add enough pixels for bleed and cropping, but avoid massive unused resolution.

Use JPG for photographic images when transparency is not needed. Use PNG carefully for line art or transparent elements, but avoid giant transparent PNG canvases on every page if the page can be flattened. For black-and-white coloring pages, clean line art at the right print size usually beats oversized AI-upscaled files.

Optimize repeated backgrounds. If every journal page uses the same faint paper texture, consider whether the texture is necessary. If it is, size it to the page and flatten it into the page design rather than stacking multiple transparent overlays.
### Flatten the PDF Before Upload
Flattening reduces render complexity. It is especially useful when the file contains shadows, glows, semi-transparent shapes, imported vector illustrations, clipping masks, or layered page art.

In Photoshop, build at final print size, keep a master layered file, then export a flattened print PDF or flattened page images at 300 DPI. In Affinity, use PDF export settings that rasterize unsupported properties while preserving text and vector quality where appropriate. In Adobe Acrobat Pro, use preflight and optimization tools to flatten transparency and clean unused objects.
Always keep an editable master file. Flatten the upload copy, not your only working file. Then open the exported PDF and inspect key pages at 200 percent zoom before uploading again.
### Re-export Using Better Settings

A clean export fixes many files that appear mysterious. In Canva, choose Share, Download, PDF Print. If your book needs bleed, enable bleed in the design and make sure backgrounds extend beyond the trim edge. Avoid PDF Standard, JPG, screenshots, and post-export resizing for KDP print files.

For professional design tools, use a print PDF preset, 300 DPI effective image resolution, embedded fonts, standard PDF compatibility, correct page boxes, and flattened transparency where needed. Do not export, compress, edit in another tool, convert to images, and convert back to PDF unless you understand exactly what each step changes.

For covers, confirm the full wrap dimensions match KDP. The cover must include back cover, spine, front cover, and bleed. If the cover is built on the wrong canvas, optimization will not solve the upload problem. See [KDP bleed vs no bleed](/blog/kdp-bleed-vs-no-bleed), [safe area checking before export](/blog/how-to-check-safe-area-before-exporting-kdp-cover), and [spine alignment troubleshooting](/blog/fix-kdp-spine-text-off-center) if the upload problem overlaps with layout warnings.
### Split-Test the Manuscript

Split-testing is the expert move when KDP manuscript upload stuck problems keep coming back. Create a temporary PDF with the first 10 pages. Upload it. If it processes, create a 50-page test. If that works, test pages 51 to 100, then continue until you find the range that fails.

This method tells you whether the whole file is too heavy or whether one page is poisonous. A single corrupted illustration, giant texture, malformed font, or AI-upscaled image can stall processing even when the rest of the manuscript is fine.
When a range fails, split it again. Test pages 51 to 75, then 76 to 100. Keep narrowing until you find the page or asset. This is much faster than guessing and re-exporting the full book ten times.
Use the same logic for covers. If the cover upload slow problem started after adding one background, effect, or barcode-adjacent graphic, remove that element in a duplicate file and test again.

Split-testing also helps you avoid false fixes. If the first 10 pages fail, the issue is probably in setup, fonts, page boxes, or a repeated master element. If pages 1 to 50 pass but pages 51 to 100 fail, you are looking for a local asset problem. If every small section passes but the full file fails, the file may be too heavy overall rather than corrupted on one page.

For interiors made in Canva, duplicate the design and delete page ranges from the duplicate for testing. For professional tools, export selected page ranges. For PDFs already exported, use Acrobat or another trustworthy PDF tool to extract page ranges without recompressing everything. Keep test files temporary and do not publish from a chopped-up manuscript.
### Remove Problematic Pages

Problem pages usually have a pattern. They contain a giant scanned texture, a transparent PNG much larger than the page, a complex AI illustration, rasterized text, a corrupted image, or a pasted PDF object from another tool.

For example, a 100-page coloring book may process normally until one mandala page exported from an AI upscaler at 9000 x 9000 pixels. A puzzle book may fail because a maze page was inserted as a screenshot from a browser. A planner may hang because one section uses a full-page transparent watercolor overlay on every sheet.

Rebuild those pages from cleaner assets. Resize the image, flatten the page, replace screenshots with original artwork, remove unnecessary transparency, and export the page again. Then rebuild the final manuscript from the corrected source.
### Upload at Off-Peak Times

Sometimes the problem is Amazon-side. KDP can experience server delays, temporary rendering failures, regional issues, or maintenance windows. Upload spikes around weekends, holidays, and launch deadlines can also make processing feel slower.

If your PDF is reasonably optimized and the same behavior appears across browsers, wait and try again later. Keep a note of the exact date, time, file name, and step where the upload froze. If you contact Amazon KDP support, that detail is more useful than saying the upload did not work.

Use trustworthy sources when you are unsure. Amazon official [KDP Help](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help) should be the source for current file rules, supported formats, and upload limits. Adobe official [PDF optimization documentation](https://helpx.adobe.com/acrobat/using/optimizing-pdfs-acrobat-pro.html) is a better reference for Acrobat optimization than random compressor advice.
## Recommended File Size Guidelines for KDP
Use these as practical working ranges, not hard Amazon rules. The right size depends on page count, image type, trim size, color mode, and export quality.
Text-heavy books: recommended under 20 MB, usually safe under 50 MB, high risk above 100 MB unless there is a clear reason.
Journals and planners: recommended 10 MB to 60 MB, usually safe under 100 MB, high risk above 150 MB when pages use repeated backgrounds.
Puzzle books: recommended 20 MB to 80 MB, usually safe under 120 MB, high risk above 180 MB when puzzles are screenshots or full-page images.
Coloring books: recommended 40 MB to 150 MB, usually safe under 200 MB, high risk above 250 MB to 300 MB, especially with full-page PNGs.
Photo books and art books: recommended 100 MB to 250 MB when images are optimized, usually safe depends on page count, high risk above 300 MB to 500 MB unless the file is professionally prepared.

A file below these ranges can still fail if it contains corrupted pages or complex transparency. A file above these ranges can sometimes pass. The ranges are meant to tell you when to stop waiting and start optimizing.

For covers, the file is usually much smaller than the manuscript. A normal paperback cover PDF might be 5 MB to 40 MB. A cover above 100 MB is unusual unless it contains a very large photo, heavy texture, or complex layered art. If KDP cover upload slow behavior starts after adding one background image, inspect that image first.

Do not chase a tiny number. A 12 MB cover can print badly if it uses compressed screenshots, while a 45 MB cover can be perfectly reasonable if it contains high-quality artwork. The practical question is whether the PDF contains useful print information or waste. Useful information is real image detail at final size, embedded fonts, correct page boxes, and required bleed. Waste is oversized pixels, hidden objects, redundant backgrounds, unflattened effects, and repeated conversions.

A good pre-upload habit is to keep three exported versions during troubleshooting: the original export, an optimized export, and a small test export. Name them clearly, such as manuscript-original-320mb.pdf, manuscript-optimized-118mb.pdf, and manuscript-test-pages-1-10.pdf. This prevents the common mistake of fixing the source file and accidentally uploading the old heavy PDF again.
## Real Example: Why a 320MB Coloring Book Failed

A typical failure looks like this: a creator makes a 110-page coloring book in Canva. Each coloring page starts as an AI-generated image. The images are upscaled, downloaded as large transparent PNGs, placed full page, and exported as PDF Print. The final PDF is 320 MB.
The upload reaches Amazon, but manuscript processing never completes. The creator tries another browser and gets the same result. The file opens locally, so it feels like KDP is broken.

The actual problem is processing weight. Most pages do not need transparent PNGs. Many images are far above 300 DPI at final print size. Several pages contain unnecessary background layers. A few pages include shadows and decorative elements that add transparency for no print benefit.

The repair is straightforward. The page art is resized to the actual trim size at 300 DPI plus bleed where needed. Transparent PNGs are flattened because the pages print on white paper. Repeated textures are removed. The Canva file is cleaned of hidden elements. The interior is re-exported as a fresh PDF Print file.
The new PDF is 118 MB. The line art still looks sharp at print size. KDP processes it successfully. Nothing about the book concept changed; only the export and asset handling changed.
## When the Problem Is Actually Amazon KDP

Do not assume every slow upload is your fault. KDP can have temporary delays. The rendering service may be overloaded. A valid file can fail once and process later. Regional routing, browser sessions, and account-side glitches can all create weird behavior.

The difference is repeatability. If a clean, modest file fails across browsers and computers, and other publishers are reporting issues, waiting may be reasonable. If only your 300 MB image-heavy PDF fails and small test PDFs work, the file is the problem.

Check [Amazon KDP Help](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help) for current instructions and use Amazon support when a file that meets requirements repeatedly fails. For PDF repair and optimization, use official Adobe guidance such as [Acrobat PDF optimization documentation](https://helpx.adobe.com/acrobat/using/optimizing-pdfs-acrobat-pro.html).

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Why is my KDP upload taking so long?
Your KDP upload is usually slow because the PDF is oversized, image-heavy, unflattened, or difficult for KDP to render. Browser memory and temporary Amazon delays can also contribute.
### What PDF size is too large for KDP?
There is no single practical cutoff for every book, but manuscripts above 150 MB to 200 MB deserve inspection. A 300 MB coloring book is a strong signal that images need optimization.
### Can Canva exports slow down KDP?
Yes. Canva exports can contain large backgrounds, duplicated assets, transparency, and oversized PNGs. PDF Print is correct, but the design still needs print-sized assets.
### Why does my upload freeze at processing?
Processing freezes when KDP can receive the file but struggles to analyze, flatten, rasterize, or render it. Test smaller page ranges to isolate the cause.
### Should I flatten my PDF before upload?
Flatten complex transparency and effects before upload, while preserving print quality. Keep an editable master file and upload a flattened copy.
### Is 600 DPI too high for KDP?
Usually, yes. Most KDP interiors and covers should use about 300 DPI at final print size. Excessive DPI makes files heavier without visible print improvement.
### How long should KDP processing normally take?
Simple books often process in minutes. Image-heavy books can take longer. If nothing changes after 20 to 30 minutes, stop waiting and troubleshoot the file.
